vignette: The concrete shudders before the sound arrives. Elias is three floors up, reviewing discovery materials in his corner office, when the floor drops. Glass rains across his desk. The air turns thick with pulverized drywall and something metallic, something burning. He doesn't think; he moves. He crawls under a heavy oak table as the world fractures. Through the haze, he sees colleagues running, the familiar blue blazers of the district attorney's office stained with dust and blood. A security guard's hand grabs his shoulder, dragging him into a stairwell. The roar follows him down each landing, a living thing that never quite leaves. He returns to work six weeks later. The courtroom still feels like a place where order should hold, where facts line up neatly and justice is a scale, not a question mark. He builds motions, cross-examines witnesses, and maps out indictments. But the architecture of the law now feels fragile. He sits in the gallery, back pressed to the wall, eyes tracking every door. When a gavel strikes, his pulse spikes. He reads police reports with clinical detachment, but his hands shake when he highlights witness statements. He tells himself he is fine. The indictment against the suspect in the courthouse bombing case should be enough. It isn't. At home, he tries to be present. His wife, Maya, sets the table with her usual care, but he notices the way her fork clinks against the porcelain and his throat closes. He watches her talk about their weekend plans and feels nothing but a hollow distance, as if someone has placed a thick pane of glass between them. He stops answering texts. He cancels dinner with friends. When the neighbor's car backfires in the driveway, he jumps so hard his knee hits the coffee table. He lies there on the rug, breathing in shallow pulls, counting the seconds until the ringing in his ears fades. Maya touches his arm, and he flinches before he can stop himself. She doesn't pull away, but he sees the hesitation in her eyes. He tells himself he is protecting her. He tells himself he is still the man who proposed to her on a pier in Maine, not the man who crawled out of a collapsed vestibule with glass in his hair. Now, his office has become a fortress of routine. He arrives early, parks on the far side of the garage, and walks the long route to his door. The case files on his desk are thick with forensic evidence, but he catches himself staring at photographs of shredded seats and fractured glass. He once found comfort in the predictability of precedent. Now, every detail feels like a potential trigger. He rehearses opening statements in the shower, but the words turn to ash in his mouth. He knows he is supposed to be the steady voice, the one who brings chaos into sequence. Instead, he sits in his chair and listens to the HVAC system hum, wondering if he is waiting for another wave of pressure. He watches the clock. He checks the lock on his office door. He breathes. He tries.
